identity.title: RF433 Remote-Control Car
identity.tagline: A dedicated joystick remote and a driven car, talking over plain 433MHz radio — no phone required.

goal: Build a genuine two-piece remote-control system: a handheld transmitter with its own Arduino and joystick, and a separate car with its own Arduino, motor driver, and receiver — communicating over a cheap 433MHz radio link instead of Bluetooth or a wire.
simpleSummary: Build a two-part remote control car using a cheap long-range radio instead of Bluetooth.
howItWorks: Unlike the Bluetooth RC Car (which pairs an existing phone to a single Arduino), this project uses two separate microcontrollers that have never met each other except through radio: a transmitter Arduino reads the joystick and broadcasts a small labeled packet of data continuously, and a receiver Arduino listens for that packet and acts on whatever it last received. RF433 transmitter/receiver pairs are extremely simple radios — they have no built-in addressing, pairing, or error-correction of their own, which is why this project uses the RadioHead library's RH_ASK driver to add basic packet framing and error-checking on top of the raw radio link, rather than trying to send meaningful data over it directly.
toolsNeeded: Arduino IDE (free, installed on your computer)
USB cable to connect the board to your computer
A second Arduino for the handheld transmitter
Small Phillips screwdriver for chassis assembly

components.note: one for the remote, one for the car
TX on the remote, RX on the car
powers the car; the remote can run from a USB battery bank or a 9V battery
a full assortment across both units

circuitDiagramCaption: Two independent builds linked only by radio: a remote (joystick + TX) and a car (RX + L298N + motors + battery).

wiringSteps.instruction: On the remote's Arduino, wire the joystick's VCC/GND to 5V/GND, VRx to A0, VRy to A1.
wiringSteps.detail: Same joystick wiring as Joystick Pan-Tilt Turret.

wiringSteps.instruction: On the remote's Arduino, wire the RF433 transmitter module's DATA pin to D12, VCC to 5V, and GND to GND.
wiringSteps.detail: Transmitter modules typically have an antenna pad or a short wire leg — a simple ~17cm straight wire soldered there noticeably improves range over no antenna at all.

wiringSteps.instruction: On the car, build the chassis and motor wiring exactly as in the Line-Following Robot: motors to L298N OUT1-4, Arduino D2-D5 to IN1-4, D6/D9 to ENA/ENB, battery to +12V/GND, and that ground shared with the car's Arduino.
wiringSteps.detail: Identical motor-driver wiring to every other L298N-based project in this encyclopedia.

wiringSteps.instruction: On the car's Arduino, wire the RF433 receiver module's DATA pin to D12, VCC to 5V, GND to GND.
wiringSteps.detail: Receiver modules are pickier about power stability than transmitters — a small capacitor across its VCC/GND can help if readings seem unreliable.

wiringSteps.instruction: Install the RadioHead library (search "RadioHead" in the Arduino Library Manager) on both Arduinos before uploading their respective sketches.
wiringSteps.detail: Each Arduino gets a different sketch — don't upload the same code to both.

code.explanation: commandFromJoystick() collapses the joystick's two continuous axis readings down to the same single-letter command vocabulary (F/B/L/R/S) used by the Bluetooth RC Car project, just decided locally on the remote instead of typed into a phone app. driver.send() hands that one character to RadioHead, which wraps it with framing and a checksum before it goes out over the raw radio link — sending it repeatedly, ~10 times a second, means the car always has a very recent command even though this simple radio link has no acknowledgment of receipt.

driver.recv() checks for a freshly arrived, checksum-valid packet without blocking, similar in spirit to the Bluetooth car's bluetooth.available(). The COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS safety check is the one genuinely new idea compared to the Bluetooth version: because this simple radio link can silently drop packets or lose range with no notification, the car deliberately stops itself if half a second passes without a fresh command, rather than barreling ahead forever on the last instruction it happened to receive.

expectedBehavior: Moving the remote's joystick in any direction drives the car the same way in real time; releasing the joystick back to center stops it. Walking the remote out of range, or turning it off, causes the car to stop within half a second rather than continuing blindly.

troubleshooting.issue: Car never responds to the remote at all.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm both modules have an antenna wire (even a short straight wire helps enormously over none), and that both sketches were uploaded to the correct Arduino — mixing up transmitter and receiver code is an easy first mistake.

troubleshooting.issue: Car responds erratically or randomly changes direction.
troubleshooting.fix: This is usually radio interference from other 433MHz devices nearby (garage door remotes, weather stations) — RH_ASK's checksum should reject most garbage, but very strong nearby interference can still overwhelm short-range hobby modules.

troubleshooting.issue: Range is much shorter than expected.
troubleshooting.fix: Add a proper ~17cm antenna wire to both modules if you haven't already — this single change is by far the biggest range improvement available on these modules.

troubleshooting.issue: Car doesn't stop when the remote is turned off.
troubleshooting.fix: Confirm COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS logic is intact in the receiver sketch — without it, the car has no way to know the remote has gone away and will simply continue its last command.

extensions: Add a second joystick axis or button on the remote for variable speed instead of one fixed SPEED.
Add a status LED on the car that blinks when it hasn't received a command recently (before the timeout triggers a full stop).
Upgrade to nRF24L01 modules for two-way communication, so the remote could receive telemetry (like battery level) back from the car.
Compare this build directly against the Bluetooth RC Car project — same driving logic, completely different wireless link and range/reliability trade-offs.
